Appendix B Tuning the strength of ℒalign\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}
[id=A2.p1.1] In this appendix, we look at the impact of the alignment loss, and how to tune its strength—which we call β\beta in this section. We consider the CLIP model, and train a family of SAEs with β\beta ranging from 10−510^{-5} to 10−210^{-2} on a logarithmic scale. The alignment loss is defined by the average cosine similarity between matching image–caption codes :
[id=A2.E4]
ℒalign​(Z~(d)⏟∈ℝb×K,Z~(d′)⏟∈ℝb×K)=−1b​Tr​(Z~(d)⋅Z~(d′)⊤)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}(\underbrace{\widetilde{Z}^{(\textmd{d})}}_{\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times K}},\underbrace{\widetilde{Z}^{(\textmd{d}^{\prime})}}_{\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times K}})=-\frac{1}{b}\mathrm{Tr}(\widetilde{Z}^{(\textmd{d})}\cdot\widetilde{Z}^{(\textmd{d}^{\prime})\top})
(4)
[id=A2.p2.1] where bb is the batch size, KK is the number of latent concept dimensions and Z~(d)\widetilde{Z}^{(\textmd{d})} and Z~(d′)\widetilde{Z}^{(\textmd{d}^{\prime})} are normalized codes.
[id=A2.p3.1] We observe a sharp transition, with almost no effect below β=10−4\beta=10^{-4}, and systematic degenerate solutions above β=10−3\beta=10^{-3}. Figure 7 shows the evolution of reconstruction error against β\beta. At the transition, constant features start appearing with frequencies of 1. These features are degenerate solutions to the alignment loss. Figure 8 shows the proportion of energy contained in bimodal and degenerate features against β\beta.

Appendix C Toy Data Generating Process
[id=A3.SS1]
C.1 DGP definition
[id=A3.SS1.p1.1] For our toy Data Generating Process (DGP), we created two ground truth dictionaries D1,D2D_{1},D_{2} and sparse codes Z1,Z2Z_{1},Z_{2} such that Z1​D1=Z2​D2Z_{1}D_{1}=Z_{2}D_{2}. The goal is to have a realistic-enough distribution on which we have full control of which features are ”unimodal ” and which are ”bimodal ”. (D1,Z1)(D_{1},Z_{1}) will have ”ground truth” bimodal features while (D2,Z2)(D_{2},Z_{2}) will contain ”ground truth” unimodal features. One parameter, τ1\tau_{1} controls smoothly the separation between these, with no ambiguity over which of the two is the ”true” ground truth when this parameter is extreme. When τ1\tau_{1} is close to 11—resp. τ2\tau_{2}—(D1,Z1)(D_{1},Z_{1})—resp. (D2,Z2)(D_{2},Z_{2})— is the ground truth dictionary, without ambiguity. Below is the list of parameters :
[id=A3.I1.i1] •
[id=A3.I1.i1.p1.1] dd, the dimension of the latent space.
[id=A3.I1.i2] •
[id=A3.I1.i2.p1.1] kk, controlling the number of concepts, such that (D1,Z1)(D_{1},Z_{1}) has 10​k10k concepts and (D2,Z2)(D_{2},Z_{2}) has 14​k14k concepts.
[id=A3.I1.i3] •
[id=A3.I1.i3.p1.1] LL : the sparsity of the codes, such that ∀i,L0​(Z2,i)=L\forall i,L_{0}(Z_{2,i})=L.
[id=A3.I1.i4] •
[id=A3.I1.i4.p1.1] τ1\tau_{1} : controls the cosine similarity between D2ID_{2}^{I} and D2TD_{2}^{T}, such that ∀i,D2,iI,⊤⋅D2,iT=τ1\forall i,D_{2,i}^{I,\top}\cdot D_{2,i}^{T}=\tau_{1}
[id=A3.I1.i5] •
[id=A3.I1.i5.p1.1] τ2\tau_{2} : controls the cosine similarity between a matching image-caption pair, such that ∀i,(Z2,iI​D2)⊤​(Z2,iT​D2)=τ2\forall i,(Z_{2,i}^{I}D_{2})^{\top}(Z_{2,i}^{T}D_{2})=\tau_{2}
[id=A3.SS1.p3.1] where the superscript ⋅I\cdot^{I} indicates that we take the submatrices corresponding to image codes in ZZ or to image-only features in DD. Similarly for ⋅T\cdot^{T} and text.
[id=A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1]
(D1,Z1)(D_{1},Z_{1}).
[id=A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] Let DID^{I} and DTD^{T} be subsets of concepts of size kk each and corresponding to high-energy high-frequency unimodal concepts. Let DBD^{B} be 4​k4k bimodal concepts, associated to small (depending on τ1\tau_{1}) additional terms DB,ID^{B,I} and DB,TD^{B,T} of size 4​k4k each. These additional terms are modality-specific and control for the fact that features can have some amount of unimodal information.
[id=A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] We enforce that all features in DID^{I} are orthogonal to all features in DTD^{T}, DBD^{B} and DB,TD^{B,T}, similarly for DB,ID^{B,I}, DTD^{T} and DB,TD^{B,T}. All features in DBD^{B} are thus orthogonal to all features not in DBD^{B}.
[id=A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1] To generate one sample Z1,iZ_{1,i}, we proceed as follows. We select exactly one feature in DID^{I} and one in DTD^{T} that will have an activation of 11 (temporarily). Then, we select L−1L-1 features in DBD^{B}, and their corresponding additional terms in DB,ID^{B,I} and DB,TD^{B,T}. The activations associated to DBD^{B} are constant, as are those in DB,ID^{B,I} and DB,TD^{B,T}, and equal to τ1​β\tau_{1}\beta and (1−τ1)​β(1-\tau_{1})\beta respectively. To compute β\beta, we select the only positive real-valued root of the underlying 4th-degree polynomial to satisfy the constraint given by τ2\tau_{2}. Finally, we scale all activations by 1‖Z1,i​D1‖\frac{1}{\left\|Z_{1,i}D_{1}\right\|} such that the final embeddings have unit norm.

Activation strengths in Z2Z_{2} associated to BIB^{I} and BTB^{T} are unchanged, and those associated to τ1​DB+(1−τ1)​DB,I/T\tau_{1}D^{B}+(1-\tau_{1})D^{B,I/T} are equal to β\beta.

C.2 Experiments
[id=A3.SS2.p1.1] In this section, we investigate the impact of enforcing our alignment penalty ℒalign\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}} on the learned dictionaries. For that, we design two toy datasets sampled from two different data-generating processes (DGPs), one satisfying the Iso-Energy Assumption and one violating it. In both cases, parameters of the DGPs are chosen such that the data distribution is similar to the actual data distribution of LAION-400M embedded by CLIP ViT-B/32. Details on the DGPs and the datasets are given in Section C.1.
[id=A3.SS2.p2.1] We train our SAEs using the same number of atoms and sparsity as those of the DGPs. We do not report sparse reconstruction metrics, as they are all equally good, with R2≥0.99R^{2}\geq 0.99 and fixed sparsity.
[id=A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1]
Experiment 1.
[id=A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] In our first experiment, we show that both SAE and SAE-A are equally able to find the ground truth dictionary in a setup where the Iso-Energy Assumption is violated. In other words, we check that enforcing the alignment penalty does not lead to learning spurious bimodal features.
[id=A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] Let DD and ZZ be the learned dictionary and sparse codes, respectively. Let WW and CC be the ground truth dictionary weights and corresponding sparse codes, respectively. We measure the proximity between both dictionaries using the Wasserstein distance 𝒲⁡(D,W)\mathcal{W}(D,W) between the ground truth and the learned dictionary’s atoms. We also measure the mean matching accuracy mma⁡(Z,C)\mathrm{mma}(Z,C), for a permutation matrix Π∈ℝK×K\Pi\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K} that best matches the atoms in ZZ and CC. mma⁡(Z,C)\mathrm{mma}(Z,C) is the average cosine similarity between matched atoms’ activation patterns in ZZ and CC.
[id=A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1] Results are summarized in Table 5(a). We observe no distinction between the two SAEs. In particular, we show that adding the alignment penalty ℒalign\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}} does not incentivize SAE-A to learn spurious bimodal features.
[id=A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2]
Experiment 2.
[id=A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] In our second experiment, the DGP from which the data is sampled satisfies the Iso-Energy Assumption. In this case, we observe that training a SAE fails to uncover the ground truth dictionary and learns spurious, unimodal features, while training a SAE-A succeeds at doing so.
Results are summarized in Table 5(b).

Appendix D Model-dex
[id=A4.p1.1] We studied a collection of models, varying in size and training procedure from the CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023), and OpenCLIP (Cherti et al., 2023) implementations.
[id=A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
CLIP and OpenCLIP.
[id=A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We used the ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 variants of both CLIP and OpenCLIP. These were trained with the contrastive softmax loss to align matching pairs and separate non-matching ones. Specifically, we used openai/clip-vit-base-patch32, openai/clip-vit-large-patch14, laion/CLIP-ViT-B-32-laion2B-s34B-b79K and laion/CLIP-ViT-L-14-laion2B-s32B-b82K from hugging face’s transformers.CLIPModel implementation. They are referred to as CLIP, CLIP-L, OpenCLIP, and OpenCLIP-L.
[id=A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2]
SigLIP.
[id=A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We conducted our experiments using both SigLIP, trained with a sigmoid-based contrastive loss, and SigLIP2, trained with a heterogeneous mix of objectives. Specifically, we used google/siglip-base-patch16-224 and google/siglip2-base-patch16-224 from hugging face’s transformers.SiglipModel implementation.
[id=A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1] We report in Figure 10 linear projections of embeddings, colored by modality, illustrating the modality gap. We measure the modality gap both as the Difference in Mean (DiM) between each modality and as the difference in distribution, with the Wasserstein distance (𝒲\mathcal{W}). We repeat this on three datasets (Appendix J). We report the modality gap inside of each dataset in Table 6.
[id=A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1] Finally, we report recall@1 and recall@5, along with histograms of cosine similarities between embeddings of the same modality, matching embeddings of different modalities, and random pairs of embeddings of different modalities in Figures 11 and 6. We add a histogram of cosine similarity between samples from white noise as a reference.
[id=A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p4.1] For the ImageNet dataset, we also measure zero-shot recall—slightly different from recall@1, see Appendix E—and classifier accuracy.

E.1 VLM encoder metrics
[id=A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1]

[id=A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] Let I,T∈Rb×dI,T\in R^{b\times d} be normalized embeddings of matching image and captions. Let C=I⋅T⊤∈[−1,1]b×bC=I\cdot T^{\top}\in[-1,1]^{b\times b} be the matrix of cosine similarities between these embeddings. Let 𝒍\bm{l} be the vector of ground truth matching labels : 𝒍=⟦0,b−1⟧∈ℕb\bm{l}=\llbracket 0,b-1\rrbracket\in\mathbb{N}^{b}, and topk(img)∈ℕb×k\mathrm{topk}^{(\mathrm{img})}\in\mathbb{N}^{b\times k} be such that topki,j(img)\mathrm{topk}^{(\mathrm{img})}_{i,j} is the jj-th best match for the image embedding ii, and likewise for topk(txt)\mathrm{topk}^{(\mathrm{txt})}. We can now define recall​@​k=12​b​∑i(𝟏i∈topki(img)+𝟏i∈topki(txt))\mathrm{recall@k}=\frac{1}{2b}\sum_{i}\left(\bm{1}_{i\in\mathrm{topk}^{(\mathrm{img})}_{i}}+\bm{1}_{i\in\mathrm{topk}^{(\mathrm{txt})}_{i}}\right). In other words, it measures the accuracy of the model at matching image-caption pairs.
As this metric depends on the batch size bb, we will fix it to 256256 throughout this study.
[id=A5.SS1.SSS0.Px2]
Zero-shot accuracy.
[id=A5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] The goal of this metric is to measure the quality of multimodal embeddings through downstream task performance. In the context of image classification, text embeddings are constrained to a small number of points, corresponding to simple descriptions of the class—e.g., ”an image of a {class}”. Following Radford et al. (2021), we generate about 80 text descriptions for each ImageNet class, embed them, take their average, and finally normalize this average to get the class classifier. By concatenating all of these embeddings, we get a linear classifier, and zero-shot accuracy is the accuracy of this classifier. As for recall, ”@k” means that the prediction is correct if the correct class is among the kk best matches.
[id=A5.SS1.SSS0.Px3]
Classifier Accuracy.
[id=A5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] Alternatively, we train a linear classifier on the image embeddings instead of taking the one given by the embedding of these basic textual class descriptions. This metric doesn’t consider the multimodal aspect of the embeddings anymore; it only considers whether the embeddings contain the information to classify.
[id=A5.SS1.SSS0.Px4]
Retrieval.
[id=A5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] We evaluate retrieval performance, another downstream task, on the FashionIQ dataset (Appendix J). To do so, we consider the average of recall@10 and recall@50, as in Wu et al. (2021). Instead of matching images II and texts TT, we now have queries QQ and targets TT. Queries are functions of the source image’s embedding and the relative caption’s embedding, typically the normalized sum. Targets are the target image’s embedding.
[id=A5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p2.1] The goal is to quantify the quality of semantic vector arithmetic. Qualitatively, the embedding of an image of a red shoe 𝒊src\bm{i}_{\mathrm{src}} plus the embedding of the relative description ”is not red but blue” 𝚫\bm{\Delta} should match the embedding of an image of a blue shoe 𝒊src+𝚫∼𝒊trg\bm{i}_{\mathrm{src}}+\bm{\Delta}\sim\bm{i}_{\mathrm{trg}}. Quantitatively, we evaluate both if our queries have high recall—meaning they can retrieve images of blue shoes—and whether they belong to the distribution of images—meaning they are actually embeddings of blue shoes—using the distance to the K-th Nearest Neighbor, a standard out-of-distribution (OOD) detection method (Sun et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022).

[id=A5.I2.i1.p1.1] Interventions: C−insertionC\mathrm{-insertion}, C−deletionC\mathrm{-deletion} (Fel et al., 2023a) We include these metrics for completeness, even though they are not very useful in our case. For all data points, they sort active features by attribution and either insert or delete them one by one, measuring the downstream effect.
Attribution is relative to a scalar, and we used the reconstruction error in this case. This is not very informative, as activation is then a very good proxy for attribution due to the near orthogonality of features. What these metrics tell us is essentially how fast the activation decreases if you sort features by activation.
An arguably more useful way of computing these metrics would have been w.r.t. the cosine similarity between matching pairs or w.r.t. the recall. But again, it would not be very informative, and they would essentially become weaker versions of δr​@​1\delta_{\mathrm{r@1}}.

[id=A11]
Appendix K Why remove bias before comparing content
[id=A11.p1.1] One could ask why it is important to remove unimodal information and what impact this has on retrieval and other downstream tasks. Can it help improve performance by cleaning the representation and revealing the useful semantic information? Building on the fact that many works have found that modality-specific components live in orthogonal subspaces, we are left with two choices: either the modality information acts as a constant offset, in which case removing or adding it does not change rankings, or the modality information is adaptive, as we find in this work. In the adaptive case, retrieval rankings can change significantly, making our decomposition a useful tool for precise control and steering of retrieval systems.
We detail this here, and start with our setup.
[id=A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
Setup
[id=A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We work in a representation space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} that decomposes orthogonally as ℝd=Γ⊕Ω\mathbb{R}^{d}=\Gamma\oplus\Omega into a content subspace Γ\Gamma and a modality subspace Ω\Omega with Γ⟂Ω\Gamma\perp\Omega. For any underlying item 𝒙\bm{x}, the observed embedding factorizes as
[id=A11.Ex4]
𝒗=𝝎⁡(𝒙)⏟modality ∈Ω+𝜸⁡(𝒙)⏟content ∈Γwithℝd=Γ⊕Ω\bm{v}=\underbrace{\bm{\omega}(\bm{x})}_{\text{modality }\in\Omega}+\underbrace{\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x})}_{\text{content }\in\Gamma}\quad\text{with}\quad\mathbb{R}^{d}=\Gamma\oplus\Omega
[id=A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2] where 𝝎⁡(𝒙)∈Ω\bm{\omega}(\bm{x})\in\Omega captures modality-specific information and 𝜸⁡(𝒙)∈Γ\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x})\in\Gamma represents the semantic content estimated by our SAE. The orthogonal direct sum decomposition ensures that content and modality components are geometrically independent.
[id=A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] For retrieval, we score against a set of unit-normalized candidates {𝒚i}i=1n\{\bm{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} using cosine similarity. To analyze pairwise rankings, we define the content margin Δc​(i,j)≔⟨𝜸⁡(𝒙),𝒚i−𝒚j⟩\Delta_{c}(i,j)\coloneqq\langle\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}-\bm{y}_{j}\rangle and the modality margin Δm​(i,j)≔⟨𝝎⁡(𝒙),𝒚i−𝒚j⟩\Delta_{m}(i,j)\coloneqq\langle\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}-\bm{y}_{j}\rangle. We also write αi≔⟨𝝎⁡(𝒙),𝒚i⟩\alpha_{i}\coloneqq\langle\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle for the modality projection onto candidate ii.
[id=A11.SS1]
K.1 Constant modality information
[id=A11.SS1.p1.1] We first consider the case where modality information affects all candidates equally. This corresponds to the intuitive scenario where modality acts as a simple offset that shifts all similarities by the same amount, leaving relative rankings unchanged.
[id=A11.SS1.p2.1] When the modality component 𝝎⁡(𝒙)\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}) projects with identical strength onto every candidate in the retrieval set, removing this component preserves all pairwise orderings. This formalizes the intuition that a candidate-independent offset cannot affect relative rankings.
Proposition 2 (Ranking invariance under constant projection).
[id=Thmproposition2.p1.1] Assume unit normalized candidates {𝐲i}i=1n\{\bm{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}. If there exists α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} such that ⟨𝛚⁡(𝐱),𝐲i⟩=α\langle\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle=\alpha for all ii, then for any ii and jj
[id=A11.Ex5]
cos(𝒗,𝒚i)>cos(𝒗,𝒚j)⇔cos(𝜸(𝒙),𝒚i)>cos(𝜸(𝒙),𝒚j)\cos(\bm{v},\bm{y}_{i})>\cos(\bm{v},\bm{y}_{j})\quad\iff\quad\cos(\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i})>\cos(\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{j})
[id=Thmproposition2.p1.2] The same equivalence holds with equality. The statement also holds for dot product scoring.

[id=A11.SS1.p3.1] With ‖𝒚i‖=1\|\bm{y}_{i}\|=1 we have

cos⁡(𝒗,𝒚i)=⟨𝒗,𝒚i⟩‖𝒗‖=⟨𝝎⁡(𝒙),𝒚i⟩+⟨𝜸⁡(𝒙),𝒚i⟩‖𝒗‖\cos(\bm{v},\bm{y}_{i})=\frac{\langle\bm{v},\bm{y}_{i}\rangle}{\|\bm{v}\|}=\frac{\langle\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle+\langle\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle}{\|\bm{v}\|}
[id=A11.SS1.p4.1] Under the hypothesis ⟨𝝎⁡(𝒙),𝒚i⟩=α\langle\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle=\alpha for all ii we get

cos⁡(𝒗,𝒚i)−cos⁡(𝒗,𝒚j)=α−α‖𝒗‖+⟨𝜸⁡(𝒙),𝒚i⟩−⟨𝜸⁡(𝒙),𝒚j⟩‖𝒗‖=Δc​(i,j)‖𝒗‖\cos(\bm{v},\bm{y}_{i})-\cos(\bm{v},\bm{y}_{j})=\frac{\alpha-\alpha}{\|\bm{v}\|}+\frac{\langle\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle-\langle\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{j}\rangle}{\|\bm{v}\|}=\frac{\Delta_{c}(i,j)}{\|\bm{v}\|}

[id=A11.SS1.p7.1] In the constant modality regime, removing modality information yields only the subspace of interest, and potentially more interpretable multimodal embeddings, but without any performance gains or losses.
Thus, in that case, the decomposition provides the content representation by eliminating modality-specific artifacts, but since rankings remain identical, one should not expect improvements in retrieval metrics. This case represents a neutral scenario where the primary benefit is representational clarity rather than functional enhancement.

[id=A11.SS1.p11.1] This corollary establishes a robustness condition: when modality variations are small relative to content differences—even in the presence of multiple adaptive modality components – the content signal prevails and rankings remain unchanged. [id=A11.SS1.p12.1] However, as we will show next and as we empirically find in this work, real modality information is typically adaptive rather than constant, leading to significant ranking changes when removed.

K.2 Adaptive modality information
[id=A11.SS2.p1.1] This is what we observe empirically in this work. The modality signal decomposes into multiple unimodal atoms and the modality projection varies significantly across candidates. In this regime, removing 𝝎⁡(𝒙)\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}) can dramatically change rankings. The next proposition provides a necessary and sufficient condition for ranking flips and clarifies that flips occur when the candidate-dependent modality margin opposes and dominates the content margin.
